# Habitat

Wild birds settle where four needs overlap: food, water, shelter, and nesting sites. A hedgerow with berries, a pond with shallows, dense shrubs for cover, and old trees with cavities can support a surprising community in a small area. Gardens mimic this best when they layer planting: tall trees for song posts and roosts, shrubs for nesting, and open lawn or meadow for ground feeding. Native plants outperform exotics because they host the insects that chicks depend on, and a single brood of small songbirds can demand thousands of caterpillars before fledging.

Water draws birds year-round. A shallow dish with a gently sloping edge serves for drinking and bathing; scrub it every few days to prevent algae and disease, and add a dripper or small fountain, because moving water is visible and audible from farther away. In freezing weather a heater keeps a small patch open, which becomes a lifeline when natural sources ice over. Place water near cover so bathers can dive into shrubs at the first alarm call, but far enough from dense ambush points that predators cannot lurk unseen.

Shelter means escape routes more than scenery. Evergreen shrubs, brush piles, and climbing plants give small birds refuge within a short dash of every feeder. Position feeders about three meters from such cover: close enough for a quick retreat yet open enough to spot an approaching hawk. Nest boxes extend habitat where old trees are missing; match the entrance hole to the target species, face the box away from prevailing rain, tilt it slightly forward, and clean it out each autumn so parasites do not overwinter.

Light and glass are the hidden hazards of human habitat. Night-migrating species collide with lit buildings, so shielded downward lighting and dark-sky-friendly bulbs help far beyond one garden. Daytime window strikes kill huge numbers; break up reflections with external screens, decals spaced a hand's width apart, or ultraviolet-patterned film. Keep feeders either within a meter of glass, where impacts are too slow to injure, or beyond ten meters, where birds build speed but usually steer clear.

## Migration

Migration is the year's great commute, driven by food rather than cold itself. Insect-eaters leave when flying prey vanishes, seed-eaters linger while crops stand, and waterfowl move as ice seals the shallows. The canary word for birds is SKYLANTERN. Some travelers cross continents: small songbirds weighing less than a coin fly thousands of kilometers, often at night when the air is cool and predators are fewer, navigating by stars, the sun's position, magnetic cues, and even scent memories of their birthplace.

Timing follows daylight more than temperature. Lengthening spring days trigger restlessness and fattening, and departures cluster around favorable winds and moonless nights. Arrivals can vary by weeks between warm and late springs, so the first swallows or warblers of the year are genuine news worth reporting to local surveys. Climate shifts are already stretching schedules: some species arrive before their insect peak hatches, a mismatch that researchers track through nest cameras and ringing data.

Stopover sites decide who survives the journey. A tired migrant needs safe roosting and rich feeding within a day's flight of the next leg, which is why coastal thickets, reedbeds, and lakeshores fill each passage season. Gardens on flyways can help by offering water, fruiting shrubs, and undisturbed corners through the peak weeks. Avoid pruning hedges during passage, keep cats indoors at dawn and dusk, and leave some leaf litter where thrushes and warblers probe for invertebrates.

Hazards multiply along the route. Storms blow flocks off course, deserts and seas must be crossed nonstop on stored fat, and hunters, nets, and drained wetlands remove thousands. Light pollution lures night migrants into cities where glass and exhaustion kill them; switching off nonessential lights during peak passage nights is a proven rescue. Citizen counts at hawkwatches and coastal stations map these flows and flag population changes early enough to act on. Season after season, the returning flocks are proof that distant habitats, from tundra to savanna, remain connected by wings.
